newsitem.title: USA: Dangers may lurk in space station module - NASA.
newsitem.headline: Dangers may lurk in space station module - NASA.

text.p: Deadly chemicals, broken glass and other dangers may be lurking behind the hatch of the crash-damaged science module at the Mir space station, a NASA official said on Monday.
"I am sure the Russians are just as concerned as we are about what's in there and what the hazards might be," said Frank Culbertson, the veteran shuttle commander who runs NASA's missions to Mir.

NASA officials were worried about the danger from shards of broken glass and deadly chemicals such as formaldehyde used in biology experiments, saying they could enter the rest of the space station after a planned spacewalk to restore some power to Mir.
"It conjures up a picture that you would only find in a science fiction movie," said Craig Covault, senior space technology editor at the trade journal 'Aviation Week'.
"A U.S.-Russian space crew opens up a dead space station module not knowing what hazards lie behind the door."

Mir commander Vasili Tsibliev and Alexander Lazutkin are to attempt to tap power from the damaged module's electricity-generating solar panels during a risky spacewalk, planned for no earlier than July 17.
The repair will restore only 20-30 percent of the power lost in the crash because the damaged module's solar panels will not turn to follow the sun.
"We shouldn't be overly optimistic on how much power they are going to be able to regain," Culbertson said.

The U.S. and Russian space authorities were nearing the end of studies into the possible dangers inside the Spektr science module, which lost air pressure after its hull was ruptured when a cargo craft ploughed into the station last month.

NASA engineers were also investigating if a space shuttle docked at Mir could be exposed to dangerous chemicals leaking from the module. There may also be risks for a four-hour spacewalk planned for the next shuttle docking in September.
"We do have contamination concerns and we are looking at that very carefully," Culbertson said.
A power shortage had delayed the opening of the Progress cargo craft which docked at Mir early Monday. The space station's crew were to start unloading the resupply ship in the coming hours.
